# **Executive Summary** {#executive-summary}

The risk to our observatories' detector controller reliability has increased significantly in the past 24 months because of an event that has resulted in unexpected equipment obsolescence of a much-used controller type. This risk is further amplified by the uncontrolled diversification of controller technologies across 60+ active instruments under NOIRLab’s responsibility(1) and by the need to plan for future instrumentation. Based on internal and external consultations with peer groups facing similar challenges, we conclude that the best path forward is to design a new, modern, scalable, and modular controller that can serve both NOIRLab and the broader community. We have produced a high-level architectural design and an initial prototype board concept to begin this effort.

# **Scope of this Document** {#scope-of-this-document}

The purpose of this document is to **identify a cost effective and technologically appropriate method to replace obsolete electronics associated with the acquisition of scientific images from the sixty plus operational detector systems that are available to observers of the AURA observatories. This document also provides an initial pathway for the support of emerging detector technologies that will likely be required for new instrumentation**.

# **Project Background** {#project-background}

The timing of this project is especially relevant: the same singular event that increased the risk to operational reliability—the closure of Astronomical Research Cameras, Inc. (ARC), a major supplier of detector-controller equipment—has simultaneously affected other scientific organizations. Preliminary discussions with detector engineers at peer observatories indicate strong interest in a common, flexible architecture developed through open-source collaboration in design and procurement. Current interested parties include Fermilab, GMTO, Harvard, and University of Hawaii (SSEI group), and we anticipate broader collaboration as a core working group forms. This collaboration would significantly reduce development costs for replacing obsolete equipment and provide a flexible path for future instrumentation.

In addition, we currently employ several MONSOON systems on primary instruments at the Blanco and WIYN telescopes which employ many critical components that are obsolete. The required operational life of these instruments exceeds this decade. 

Compounding the risk, AURA observatories collectively operate seventeen additional, distinct controller technologies, many with limited or no spare parts and highly localized system knowledge. While not all of these systems fall directly under NOIRLab’s responsibility, NOIRLab is typically the first responder when failures or performance issues arise. Looking ahead, as new instruments are conceived and procured, we must account for the added maintenance burden of multiple detector systems, while also addressing the growing impact of obsolescence on existing systems’ maintenance and operational reliability.

## **1.2 What Can We Do About This?** {#1.2-what-can-we-do-about-this?}

**1). Do nothing.**

| *Advantages* | No additional expenditure of resources or capital. |
| :---- | :---- |
| *Disadventages* | Increasing risk of lost observing time. Possible loss of instrument availability (until repair or an ad hoc replacement is found). **Increased staff stress**. Greater diversity of equipment types, making specialization more critical as new instrumentation arrives. Does not address obsolescence of the acquisition computer (PAN), which uses the PCI bus. |

**2). Become specialists in the repair of existing equipment types.**

| *Advantages* | Improves preparedness for maintenance needs on existing equipment. Adds to the broader detector-engineering knowledge base. |
| :---- | :---- |
| *Disadventages* | Repairs are constrained by component obsolescence; many parts may be unavailable. Does not prepare for future instrumentation, increasing the overall knowledge burden. Increases staff time and resources devoted to maintenance. Still does not address obsolescence of the acquisition computer (PAN), which uses the PCI bus. |

**3). Redesign electronic boards required for maintenance to use non-obsolescent components.**

### 

| *Advantages* | Improves readiness to maintain existing equipment. |
| :---- | :---- |
| *Disadvantages* | Resource-intensive (engineering time, testing, documentation). Reinventing the wheel; does not reduce the diversity of system types. Only narrow obsolescence risk; single-point failures remain elsewhere in the chain (e.g., other boards, PAN/PCI host). In some cases, we do not have the base design and code to make necessary modifications.  The IP remains proprietary. |

**4). Buy in new controllers for those systems that become problematic.**

| *Advantages* | Defers capital spending until the system’s reliability inflection point. Minimizes in-house resource use. Let new instruments choose the most suitable controller technology. Supports incremental replacement. |
| :---- | :---- |
| *Disadvantages* | Reintroduces single-source/proprietary risk. Requires staff retraining on new equipment types. Tends to increase technology diversity; commercial offerings are rarely generic across applications. Leads to substantial capital outlay over time. |

**5). Develop in-house controller technology as a replacement for obsolescent equipment and new instrumentation.**

| *Advantages* | Brings controller technology back in-house—full control over architecture and lifecycle. Reduces technology variety and creates in-house training opportunities (local knowledge becomes organizational knowledge). Enables planned (“programmed”) obsolescence without single-source risk. Supports incremental replacement. Invests in a platform for future instrument needs. By design, simplifies maintenance and lowers long-term resource use. Strengthens talent retention through ownership of an engaging engineering project. Provides supported standardization that can be adopted across astronomy |
| :---- | :---- |
| *Disadvantages* | Requires a relatively large initial investment in staff resources and moderate capital. Lead time of \~24 months\* to reach operational status; demands foresight and planning (with potential to shorten given modern components). |

(\*) This estimation of time is based on previous efforts in these development projects however, factoring in the dramatic improvements in quality and functionality of electronic integrated circuits since these projects were finished should reduce the development time required to produce production quality controllers today.

## **1.3 Discussion** {#1.3-discussion}

### 

Among NOIRLab’s detector-technology specialists, **there is clear consensus to pursue an in-house development program—Option 5—for the next-generation detector-controller platform**.There are several reasons to support our consensus:

* **Proven Expertise in Advanced Detector Electronics**  
  * Our tradition of controller design originates from the former NOAO (ARCON and MONSOON systems), leveraging decades of architectural insights and best practices under the NOIRLab / NOAO banner.  
  * Our team has also deep, hands-on expertise designing cutting-edge electronics for    
    experimental detectors, including low-noise preamplifier PCBs for Skipper and MAS Skipper CCDs achieving sub-0.2 electron read noise—the best performance recorded on sky.  
  * This real-world, high-precision DAQ experience translates directly into a robust, low-risk path for the new controller platform.  
* **In-House Development & Maintainability**:   
  * All hardware and firmware are developed internally, ensuring deep understanding of every component, faster debugging cycles, and superior long-term maintainability.  
  * The in-house development experience passes down to newer generations. This allows the know-how to be retained inside the organization regardless of more experienced members leaving or retiring.  
* **In-House Astronomical Test Facilitie**s:  
  * We can rapidly prototype and validate modules using existing NOIRLab instrumentation infrastructure (e.g., CCD and NIR full test setups) on our electronics and detectors laboratories.  
  * After the laboratory validation, we can also perform on-sky testing at our telescope facilities. This ensures thorough performance verification in real-world conditions without additional capital investment or dependence on third-parties to validate the designs in harsher telescope environments.  
* **Collaborative, Community-Driven Model**  
  * NOIRLab provides the reference architecture; external labs contribute daughterboards via a central Git repository that uses pull requests, code reviews, and issue tracking.  
  * Community contributions accelerate feature development (e.g., new ADC front ends and timing modules) at near-zero marginal cost, while contributors retain authorship of their modules.  
* **Current lack of support for newer, bigger instrumentation:**  
  * Newer and larger instruments require far more video channels—e.g., current Skipper CCD designs use 64 or 128 channels for a single 4k×4k device, and H4RG-class NIR detectors also use 64 channels—**but there is no commercial controller that can manage this video channel count in a rational, unified way**.   
  * Today’s off-the-shelf options would require stacking multiple controllers in tight synchronization, which is complex, expensive, unreliable, and power-hungry. Notably, there is still no commercial system that can easily handle the 256 channels we already operate with MONSOON’s Newfirm; **a scalable, modular controller is required**.  
* **Much simpler and cheaper controller development than before**  
  * Advances in technology make designing a new controller markedly easier than just a few years ago. Off-the-shelf building blocks—System-on-Modules with Ethernet and FPGA/CPU hybrids, modern DC/DC converters, and fast, low-power ADCs—shorten development time while improving reliability.  
  * Communications have also advanced: we no longer need a custom PCI/PCIe host card to receive data. Commercial links are fast enough for our required rates and scale by simply adding channels, removing a major burden seen in earlier generations of controllers.

  ### **1.3.1 Extended discussion** {#1.3.1-extended-discussion}

This inclination of developing our own controller is in large measure to allow the knowledge gained from such a venture to be applied universally throughout the observatories under the umbra of the AURA authority. Historically, two previous in-house projects of this approach, ARCON controllers (CTIO 1993 \- 2016\) and MONSOON(2) (NOAO 2002 \- to date), have proved very successful in both longevity, application, and performance while being operationally reliable and maintainable due to the knowledge disbursement among geographical locations. The design skills and vision for such a project remain within the organization. Organizations with similar size and infrastructure as AURA (ESO(3) and Fermilab) build and maintain in-house detector controllers for their needs. Their experience in adopting this methodology is very successful in extracting the maximum performance from detector technology and enabling reliable operational status through the global knowledge of the systems they produce. Our objective for such a project would be to replace nine controller variants (potentially 51 controllers) with one generic type thus decreasing variability by approximately 50% whilst providing hooks for future detector technology requirements and the sidecar ASIC acquisition back end.

We do have experience in applying the methodology of option 3 (i.e. redesign of electronic boards using non-obsolescent components) from our experience in developing the Generic Pan Interface (GPI) hardware, firmware, and software (to support the obsolescence of acquisition computers with the PCI bus structure) but this approach does not generically solve the underlying problem of individual component obsolescence and acts only to address a specific obsolete component or module within the variety of controller types we maintain.

By the same token, Options 1 and 2—doing nothing or specializing in repairs—do not address obsolescence and cannot be considered to constitute a progressive strategy for future instrumentation.

Option 4—buying commercial controllers as issues arise—is common among smaller or single-site observatories and among university/contractor-built instruments, but it proliferates disparate technologies, complicates maintenance, and preserves single-source/proprietary risk. In practice, it is difficult to find a single vendor capable of replacing multiple obsolete controller types; most commercial cameras/controllers are built for narrow applications.

Along these lines, we had the immense help of a **controller’s survey done by Peter Doherty (April 2024\)**, at GMT, in the context of finding an appropriate controller for GMACS. **The full report can be reached on one of the links at Appendix A**. This extensive survey included **NGC** (ESO), **LTA** (Fermilab), **Stargrasp** (UH), **Monsoon** (NOAO), **Torrent** (NOAO), **DESI** (LBNL), **PSF** (Subaru), **HSC** (Subaru), **Spectral Instruments**, **Archon** (STA) and the **LSST** controller (Slack). The conclusion for them was that the optimum option was to develop their own controller, based on the LSST Slack controller to save them time. The bottom line is that **for them the best option was also to develop their own**. Considering this conclusion, we carried out some preliminary meetings with their group (Peter Doherty, Gustavo Rahmer) along with the Fermilab group (Javier Tiffenberg, Guillermo Fernandez) that is also interested in developing a more flexible, general controller. **This is to show that our concern, as well as our conclusion, is shared by other experts in the field**.

It is worth adding that new instrumentation supplied from university sources often favors the “homegrown” approach to detector controllers which usually results in under-optimized, undocumented, and sometimes unreliable solutions for detector controllers. This approach is understandable in the context of the university since it maximizes the involvement of their staff and students but results in a sub-optimum product for the observatory. In 2021 a community survey was carried out to determine which areas of technology NOIRLab could best serve to aid the astronomical community in building instrumentation. **The survey received responses from over 100 faculties and instrumentation groups. The primary area of technology expertise for hardware identified as the most sought after by the respondents are detectors and detector controller technology** which emphasizes the vacuum of experience and ability in these specializations within the academic sector. The results of the survey were presented to the NSF as part of the NOIRLab five-year plan for 2023-2027 in the context of the formation of an Instrument Technology Development Center (ITDC)(4)(5), and can be seen on a link on Appendix A.

## **1.4 Conclusions** {#1.4-conclusions}

All the arguments discussed on 1.3, lead us to what was stated at the beginning of the discussion: **we, detector specialists, all agree that the most cost/effective and promising solution for NOIRLab is to design a new detector controller in-house.** 

# **2.- The Proposed Controller**  {#2.--the-proposed-controller}

The new controller’s architecture must support the most extreme cases of the current instrumentation, but also be able to handle future developments. Regarding what we already have, Table 2 summarizes the minimum requirements based on the extreme cases on our current instrumentation. 

For forward-looking capacity to handle new instrumentation, we can assume channel counts consistent with emerging devices – for example, a single 4kx4k MAS skipper CCD similar to what STA is developing would require handling 128 channels; if we come up with a mosaic of only 4 of those we scale up to 512 channels, etc). Given we cannot really foresee all the new developments, the platform must be inherently **modular** and **scalable**. These two are then the most important requirements.

| Specification | Value | Instrument | Observatory |
| :---- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Bandwidth (MB/s) | 62 | Newfirm | CTIO |
| Number of channels | 256 | Newfirm | CTIO |
| Number of clocks | 138 | DEcam | CTIO |
| Number of biases | 72 | DEcam | CTIO |
| Number of detectors | 72 | DECam | CTIO |
| Maximum H2RG detectors | 4 | SCORPIO | Gemini South |
| Maximum EMCCD | 3 | CANOPUS | Gemini South |

**Table 2** \- minimum requirements of new controller to support current instrumentation

## **2.1 Functional and Performance Requirements** {#2.1-functional-and-performance-requirements}

In the next project phase, we will produce a dedicated Functional and Performance Requirements Document (FPRD). Below is a concise summary:

* **Very modular and scalable**, including (and especially) in the number of video channels supported.  
* Prefer commercially available standards wherever possible, including hardware modules.  
* Use Ethernet for communications and video data transmission to/from the host and between boards. If communication inside the board is required use a standard protocol like SPI or I2C.  
* Keep the design and construction as simple as possible: include only the functionality required to ensure optimal performance, effective hardware-debug mechanisms and detector safety.  
*  Maximize board commonality: the processing unit, power distribution, and communications module should be identical or nearly identical across boards; boards should differ only in front-end functions (e.g., video/ADCs, clocks/biases).  
* Use available commercial processing units, but design it so as not to get locked-in with a specific manufacturer or vendor.  
* Every function that can be implemented on the host computer safely, should be implemented in the host computer, including any pixel or image preprocessing, software debugging tools, etc.

## **2.2 Architectural Block Diagram** {#2.2-architectural-block-diagram}

Figure 1 shows the proposed general architecture.   
![][image1]

***Figure 1: proposed general controller architecture:** a) Ethernet protocol. b) A small, minimal backplane. c) Naturally scalable in number of boards and number of downlinks required.*

### 

### 

### **2.2.1 Communications** {#2.2.1-communications}

All boards use Ethernet to communicate both between them and with the host (blue lines in Figure 1).  
   
Historically, high-speed acquisition systems required costly fiber-optic transceivers and specialized / custom interface cards to transport data; by using standard Ethernet, we leverage commodity switches and network interface cards (NICs), eliminating the need to design and maintain custom transmission hardware and computer boards.

Using Ethernet also removes the need for a dedicated backplane protocol, simplifying each board, and it enables straightforward growth: if more boards are required, they simply connect to the switch. For video boards, a **Gigabit Ethernet** link provides roughly **110 MB/s** effective throughput; even a single connection exceeds current NOIRLab requirements (see **Table 2**; fastest is **NEWFIRM** at **62 MB/s**). Multiple video boards with N channels each can share the same switch and still operate with a single host downlink. For future multi-channel, faster systems (e.g., H4RG arrays or multiple Skipper devices with many channels each), adding a second switch and a second downlink—as shown by the grayed-out shapes in **Figure 1**—is straightforward and simply entails a second receiving computer. Adopting Ethernet also decouples software from any device-specific drivers or languages for data reception.

To summarize: using commercially available Ethernet transceivers and modules would provide a robust, well-tested downlink for both commands and data without custom protocols or fiber-based host boards, which always adds an important burden to the controller’s maintenance.  Ethernet is ubiquitous and backward-compatible as faster variants appear, and many SoC/SoM platforms already include mature Ethernet support. 

### **2.2.2 Backplane** {#2.2.2-backplane}

Most controllers implement a complex backplane to share signals (clocks, adc/video conversion, timing, parallel buses for the detector clocks, inter-board communications, etc). Our proposal is to reduce the backplane to a **minimal** set of lines, so the system grows naturally—just add boards, without new addresses, slots, or protocol layers. In **Figure 1**, the backplane is the orange line.

 Because inter-board communications are handled over **Ethernet**, no separate backplane protocol or board addressing is required (beyond IP). Synchronization relies on distributing a single master clock and running (largely) the same code on each board; if all boards start on the same clock edge, required signals land at the right times. Consequently, the proposed backplane has just **five logical lines**:

1) **Clock** — the master clock is shared; all other boards derive local clocks from it to remain in phase.  
2) **Sync** — asserts image-readout start; can be pulse or level.  
3) **DC power** — likely **\+12 V** input from which each board derives its power rails.   
4) **Enable** — a daisy-chain interlock returned to the master: a fixed 3.3 V or 5 V level that every board receives and re-generates. Any board fault pulls the line low, propagating a system-wide safe state to protect the detector.  
5) **GND return**.

This hybrid approach removes a data backplane, simplifies mechanics, and adds robust system-level fault detection. These are *logical* lines; physically, there may be multiples (e.g., several VCC and GND conductors).

### **2.2.2 Boards** {#2.2.2-boards}

Each board should have a narrowly defined purpose; avoid complex, multipurpose designs. Video boards handle only the detector analog front end and ADC conversion, and pixel data must go directly to the host via the board’s own Ethernet interface—no local image-processing stage, and all the discrambling process requiered happens on the host computer. Clock boards should only generate/handle clocks; for biases, a separate board is preferred unless power or space constraints dictate otherwise. The master board’s role is limited to generating the master clock and providing general-purpose functions such as timing counters, shutter handling, PID temperature control, basic telemetry polling, and sanity checks—always over Ethernet. Clock and video boards never act as masters; they merely derive the backplane clock, so no master/slave selection hardware is needed.

Because every board includes its own Ethernet interface, the host can upload the full sequencer code directly to each board. This avoids adding system-wide sequencer responsibilities to the master and keeps the design simple.

## **2.3 Boards General Block Diagram** {#2.3-boards-general-block-diagram}

Every common functionality should be implemented identically on each board (for example, Ethernet interface, clock derivation, etc); the boards should be as similar as possible between them, so the only real difference is the specific front-end that the board implements. For example, a clock board would have the same processing unit, clock derivation and power distribution than a video board, differing only in that the video board would have an instrumentation amplifier and CDS (analog or digital) as front end, while the clock driver will have a set of analog converters and multiplexing switches. Also, since a clock or bias boards do not transmit video data, they do not require a high bandwidth, and a simpler 100 Mb/s Fast Ethernet link should be enough. **We will have an actual predefined, well-defined interface between the common areas (processing unit) and the specific FEE that the board implements.** Of course, the actual code in the processor unit may differ as needed in order to suit the specific front end the board implements.

Figure 2 shows a very simplified block diagram of a generic board. Everything above the “front end interface” is common to all boards. Note that the modules stated there are logical modules and do not necessarily correspond to separate hardware units (for example, a hardware processor unit may have embedded the comms unit or RAM, etc).

***Figure 2: general boards diagram***

### **2.3.1 Common Modules** {#2.3.1-common-modules}

Modules that are expected to be found in every board. In Figure 2, everything above the FE interface  line:

1) **Comms** — module is in charge of command/response/data, Ethernet-based.   
2) **CLK/SYNC** — module in charge of the clock derivation/synchronization from the master clock that comes from the backplane. This module also uses the SYNC signal to pass it to the processor unit when an image starts being readout, and to receive/check, re-generate and output the ENABLE signal.   
3) **Power** — this module is in charge of deriving all the required voltages based on the input master VCC (12V). It may derive from it (ideally using DC-DC converters and low power regulators) 3.3V, \+-5V, \+-15V, 2.5V, etc.  
4) **Processor unit** — This is the main (core) unit of the board. Theoretically it could be an FPGA, a real-time processor (like an ARM processor), or a commercial, widely used System-On-Module (SoM) device in some commercial daughter board format which may include several desired functionality already included and well-tested by the community (like ethernet, SPI, GPIO and RAM handling etc). This would allow for a very fast development and deployment of the core of the board. Measures need to be taken on the design as to not get stuck with a particular model or vendor, so when a model gets obsolete it is reasonably simple to replace it with a newer/different model (for example, mount the commercial board over some in-house daughter board with pre-defined input/outputs, so a change of unit only requires a re-design of the daughter board.  
5) **RAM / EEPROM** — used to store data and programs, both volatile and permanent (loaded on-boot)

   ### **2.3.2 Front End Electronics (FEE)** {#2.3.2-front-end-electronics-(fee)}

The FEE is the board-specific portion of the design. The idea will be to have a very well-defined interface between the common area and the FEE. We may have different sorts of FEE, depending on the board type or subtype. ***Note that this part is mostly already done in many controllers, so the work is mostly to update with newer components, etc, but the basic designs are all proven*** (except for what is coming in new detectors, of course, but for obsolescence purposes there is not much to redesign). The most commonly used FEEs are:

#### ***2.3.2.1 Video Boards*** {#2.3.2.1-video-boards}

1) ***Optical video boards** (CCDs):*  
   *a.1) Analog*: a classical CCD analog video chain consists of some low noise instrumentation amplifier as the first stage followed by an analog CDS (integrator) and then the ADC converter. The design may include summation nodes to compensate for offsets if the coupling is DC.  
   *a.2) Digital*: A low noise instrumentation amplifier, followed directly by the AD converter (they both should be differential).  
2) ***NIR / CMOS video boards***: Similar to the optical digital chain, the instrumentation amplifier and the ADC converter (the difference is done digitally down the line).  
   

In all the above cases, there are already well-proven designs. The output of the ADC must be serialized and sent over the Ethernet port. The FEE part of the video board can contain as many parallel channels as needed and as the board can hold (4ch for many of the current optical systems would suffice, even if you need to add more than one board to the controller. 8ch boards, by the other hand, would suffice for most NIR systems).

#### 

#### 

#### ***2.3.2.2 Clock Boards*** {#2.3.2.2-clock-boards}

The FEE will consist of the buffers and DAC converters that will hold the different clock level values, and take the bits from the sequencer (likely a GPIO from the processor unit) and convert them into control signals for the mux that will switch between the clock voltages. The design may be very simple or may include more sophisticated things like telemetry, waveform shaping, etc. In principle a regular clock board would not require Gigabit Ethernet; it could implement a cheaper comms module using a regular 100 Mb/s Ethernet.

1) Optical (CCDs): the clock levels are bipolar, usually up to 15V.  
2) NIR / CMOS: the clock levels are unipolar, usually 5V or 3.3V.

   #### ***2.3.2.3 Bias Boards*** {#2.3.2.3-bias-boards}

The biases consist simply of several buffer amplifiers that polarize the detector outputs, needing to provide enough current to feed the output of the detectors. Sometimes the biases are provided by the clock driver or the video board itself. Following our approach to simplicity, unless it is due to power/space constraints, we would recommend having it as a separate board, which allows for more flexibility and space for more/better telemetry. A separate bias board would not require Gigabit Ethernet, nor a full SoM; it could implement a cheaper comms module using a regular 100 Mb Ethernet and some simpler processor unit like an industrial ARM STM32 or similar.

1) Optical (CCDs): the biases can be bipolar to accommodate for NPN and PNP detectors, usually up to 25V for regular biases, and up to 100V for substrates of fully depleted devices. The alternative is to have separate bias boards for NPN and PNP devices to make them simpler.  
2) NIR / CMOS: usually unipolar 5V or 3.3V

   #### ***2.3.2.4 Master Board*** {#2.3.2.4-master-board}

There is typically one master board per system. Unlike the others, its CLK/SYNC module generates the master clock and SYNC distributed on the backplane (rather than deriving them). Since it has no additional “master” duties, the FEE can host common utility functions such as exposure counting/shutter control, PID temperature loops, current sources for temperature sensors, and general-purpose I/O for relays or pressure sensors. The MCB should be identical across systems and may use a simpler communications module (i.e., it does not require a full 1 Gb/s link) and a modest processor unit. 

## **2.3 Sequencer/Readout** {#2.3-sequencer/readout}

The Processing unit would have a common area that implements identical functions for every board: Ethernet handling, command processing, and related services, plus a memory region where the actual sequencer code is stored.

In the simplest case, the processor code will be identical for every video and clock board. The output of the sequencer code will consist of a parallel bus (GPIO) that will produce the clocks and the conversion signals for the ADCs and video boards. Every CLK and VIDEO processor will be identical and will be running the same clock, so when an image readout starts and the SYNC signal goes high, every sequencer will run in phase, meaning that all the signals on every board will be in sync. Clock boards will generate the same clocks at the same time since the GPIO buses will be connected to clock buffers. Video boards will generate the reset/integrate/convert, etc pulses at the same time since their GPIO busses will be connected to those signals, etc. In this way everything will be synchronized without the need of one board knowing anything about the other boards. Each video will send its data through its own ethernet interface, and it will be the host’s responsibility to sort the data out based on the IP address.

In a more complex case, it would be possible for the host to distribute slightly different code to different clock boards, for example, so the clocks are distributed rather than identical (for example, one clock board only outputs the lines for the parallel clocks, and another only outputs the serial clocks, etc.

## **2.4 Architectural Notes** {#2.4-architectural-notes}

The architecture is described here in general terms. The next step would be to generate full documentation describing the functional requirements, the protocols, the hardware and software interfaces, etc.

Key design considerations/justification:

* **Modular Architecture Mitigates Obsolescence**  
  * Separation into SoM, I/O, and timing modules means individual boards can be  
    updated independently.  
  * Avoids full-controller redesign when a single component becomes obsolete.  
  * Custom or targeted daughter-card variants can be developed without changing the

  core platform.

  * Module-Specific Processor Choices: Clock sequencer modules can reuse the

  FPGA-based design; bias/low-speed modules may employ microcontrollers (e.g.,

  STM32); modules transmit at board-appropriate Ethernet speeds—e.g., low-rate

  modules at 100 Mb/s, video modules at 1 Gb/s (link-rate per board, with switch

  backbones aggregating bandwidth), and future high-bandwidth modules may

  support 10 Gb/s links.

* **SoM-Based Flexibility & Longevity**  
  * By defining only the processor-unit interface in our architecture standard, any SoM can be integrated, ensuring future migrations (e.g.,next-generation SoC or alternative modules) require minimal redesign.  
  * Long-term supply commitments from major vendors further secure availability.  
  * Vendor Roadmap Assurance: For example, AMD’s product roadmap indicates support for Zynq-7000 and RFSoC families through at least 2035, providing a ten-year technology lifecycle guarantee for our processor modules.  
* **Open-Source Toolchain & Ecosystem**  
  * We prioritize open-source and freely-available design tools.  
  * Design files—schematics, PCB layouts, HDL code—will be released under an OSI-approved license to maximize reuse, community review, and long-term maintainability.  
* **Compelling ROI and Funding Justification**  
  * Leveraging open-source and community contributions reduces direct development and QA costs.  
  * Modular updates and SoM flexibility defer replacement capital expenditure (the upfront hardware investment for new controllers) by at least 10 years per board variant.  
  * Long Service Life: Designed for a minimum of 10+ years of operation per module, this architecture minimizes obsolescence cycles and associated costs.

# 

# **3.- Board Prototype Full Design** {#3.--board-prototype-full-design}

The prototype is a **4-channel ADC video board** that exercises the proposed architecture with a real, shippable module. Each board carries its **own processor and Ethernet port** and plugs into a **minimal backplane** that only supplies 12 V power, a 10 MHz sync clock, a start/readout signal, and a fail-safe enable chain—mirroring Section 2’s Ethernet-centric design and “no data backplane” philosophy. Figure 3 shows PCB layout of the proposed video prototype board.

Physically, it’s a **162 mm × 171 mm, six-layer** impedance-controlled PCB with RJ45 **Gigabit Ethernet** (4 in Figure 3\) for configuration/telemetry/streaming and **USB-C** (9 in Figure 3\) for JTAG/UART. The video front end accepts four differential inputs (13 and 19 in Figure 3), with ±15 V available to power external preamps, matching the “video board” role defined in 2.3.2.1.

At its center is a **Trenz TE0720-04-62I33MA** **Zynq-7020 SoM** (10 in Figure 3, dual ARM® A9 \+ FPGA) with **1 GB DDR3** and **8 GB eMMC**. In this prototype the SoM (i) runs the **sequencer**, (ii) handles **Ethernet** I/O, and (iii) supervises power/sync via a cleaned 10 MHz reference—exactly the “per-board processor \+ common modules” model in 2.3. The SoM is fed a low-jitter clock from the on-board generator, and its I/O includes LVDS for the ADC link and I²C for housekeeping/ID EEPROM.

**Backplane & sync.** The board complies with the five-line backplane in 2.2.2 (2 in Figure 3, Clock, Sync, Enable, 12 V, GND). A jitter-attenuated 10 MHz input is “cleaned” and used by the sequencer and to phase-lock the DC-DC converters, while GPIO-asserted **SYNC** aligns all boards at image start—exactly the timing model in 2.3.

![][image2]  
***Figure 3: 4-Channel ADC Video Prototype PCB Board***

![][image3]  
***Figure 4: 4x5cm Trenz TE0720-04-62I33MA Zynq-7020 SoM***

**Where this lands in the architecture:**

* **Communications:** per-board **Ethernet** uplinks; no host-bus cards required.  
* **Backplane:** implements the **minimal five lines**; no data backplane, no board IDs beyond IP.  
* Uses the **common modules** pattern (Comms, CLK/SYNC, Power, Processor), with the video FEE as the only board-specific portion.  
* Four parallel channels feed the SoM; pixels stream directly to the host via Ethernet.  
* We offloaded complex DDR memory and processing to an external Zynq SoM, enabling the ADC modular board to be implemented as a streamlined 6-layer PCB—significantly reducing board complexity and fabrication cost.  
* Selected AMD Zynq 7020 combines FPGA performance and ARM processing at commodity prices. Sequencer will use FPGA time determinism while communication and video data transmission will use ARM processing capability.

The total cost of the board as well as the estimated manufacturing time is summarized in Table 3\.

| Item | Cost ($) | Mounting time (h) |
| :---- | ----- | ----- |
| Components | 890 USD | 32 |
| PCB | 250 USD | \- |

**Table 3** \- minimum requirements of new controller to support current instrumentation

Hardware schematics and PCB layouts are created in KiCad (free), and FPGA development for Zynq-7020 uses the free Vivado WebPACK edition to avoid proprietary licensing hurdles. **The full prototype schematics and full documentation are on the github link below:**

# **4.- Next Steps** {#4.--next-steps}

The immediate next step would be to manufacture the designed video board to test and refine its concepts before writing the ICDs. This involves building and independently testing each submodule (e.g., Power, Clock, Front End). The final step will be to integrate and test the complete board.

This initial phase does not include CCD testing, which requires a clock/bias board. Designing and building this second board will be simpler, as common modules will have already been tested and refined.
